title: Event-weighted variance time
lede: A price fixes total variance $w$; a volatility is $w$ divided by a clock. The event clock counts a scheduled event as extra days, so the same price reads a lower volatility.
eq_title: Expiry at calendar time $t$ in years; scheduled events $e$ on dates $t_e$
eq_labels: 1 · Variance clock: each event before expiry adds $N_e$ days
2 · Two readings of one price
3 · Optional normalisation: a one-year expiry keeps a one-year clock
eq_note: $N_e$: extra equivalent days of event $e$ ($N_e = 4$: that day counts as five). $\sigma_{\mathrm{evt}}$: the working volatility read by every fit and view. Carry, discounting and early exercise stay on calendar time $t$.
paras: Only the reading changes
prices, total variance and the butterfly and calendar checks are the same on both clocks. With no events, $\tau = t$ exactly.
After the event
its $N_e$ leaves the remaining horizon. The calendar reading falls back to the event-clock level, the vol crush; the event-clock reading does not move.
alt: Illustrative term structure: a flat 20% event-clock reading and a calendar reading that jumps where expiry crosses the event and then decays
caption: Same prices, two clocks: the event-clock reading is flat at 20%; the calendar reading jumps to 21.60% when expiry crosses the day-30 event, then decays as the event becomes a smaller share of the horizon.
example: Event on day 30 worth $N_e = 5$, 20% on the event clock. 30-day expiry: $\tau = 35/365$, $w = 0.04 \times 35/365 = 0.00384$, calendar reading $20\% \times \sqrt{35/30} = 21.60\%$. At 60 and 90 days: 20.82% and 20.55%. Normalised: every $\tau$ is multiplied by $365/370$, and the same prices read 20.14% at every expiry.
notes: An option price fixes one number: the total variance to expiry, w on the slide. That is the variance of the log-return to expiry. A volatility is that total variance divided by a length of time. The question on this slide is which length of time.

The first line is the variance clock. Event time, tau on the slide, is calendar time plus the extra days of every scheduled event on or before the expiry, divided by 365. The extra days are counted in days, never in years. An earnings day worth four extra days counts as five ordinary days. An event after the expiry adds nothing. With an empty calendar, event time equals calendar time exactly, and every fit is identical to the calendar-time pipeline.

The second line gives two readings of the same price. Total variance divided by calendar time is the calendar volatility. Total variance divided by event time is the event-clock volatility. Once an event sits inside the horizon, event time is longer than calendar time, so the event-clock reading is lower. The factor is the square root of calendar time over event time. The event-clock reading is the working one: every fit, the term view, the option table and the 3-D surface read event time.

Why bother? Measured in variance days, the diffusion looks steady again. The short-dated volatility that looks too high before earnings is the same total variance divided by too short a time. The figure shows it. On the event clock the reading is flat at 20 percent. On the calendar clock the same prices jump when the expiry crosses the event, then decay as the event becomes a smaller share of a longer horizon.

The worked example. An event on day 30, worth five extra days, and 20 percent on the event clock. A 30-day expiry has an event time of 35 over 365. Its total variance is 0.04 times 35 over 365, which is 0.00384. Divide by 30 over 365 instead and the calendar reading is 20 percent times the square root of 35 over 30: 21.60 percent. At 60 days it reads 20.82; at 90 days, 20.55.

The vol crush, read on both clocks. Once the event date has passed, its extra days are no longer ahead of the expiry. On the event clock nothing changes: 20 percent before, 20 percent after. On the calendar clock the reading falls from 21.60 toward 20. The event's variance has been delivered, and the calendar reading had been spreading it over the whole horizon.

The third line is optional and off by default. Without normalisation, events add variance to the year. With it, every day, event days included, is scaled by one factor, so that a one-year expiry reads exactly as it would with no events. Events then redistribute the year's variance instead of adding to it. With the day-30 event the factor is 365 over 370, and the same prices read 20.14 percent at every expiry.

What stays on calendar time: carry, discounting and the de-Americanisation tree all run on calendar time. Only the volatility read-off uses event time, together with every fit that works in volatility or in variance per unit of time.
Transition: typing the extra days by hand needs the date and the size of each event. The next slide reads both off the term structure.

If asked whether switching the clock changes the fit: re-reading a stored fit on another clock is exact. Changing the calendar refits the ticker, and a refit is a new calibration. The vega in the residual scales with the square root of event time, while the penalties and the vega floor do not. So the result can differ from a pure relabelling. Compare the display change and the refit separately.

If asked about intraday events: with the intraday clock on, which is off by default, maturity runs to the settlement instant. Each day accrues through a session-weighted profile. An event date is a year fraction, so an 8:30 CPI print is a fractional event date and the first line applies unchanged.
demo: Parametric ▸ Term: the Events card (date in years, extra days). The chart draws the event-clock reading and, dashed amber, the calendar reading of the same prices. Options ▸ Events and Normalize events.

title: Auto-calibrating isolated variance peaks
lede: Prices fix the forward variance between consecutive expiries. An interval that runs hotter than both neighbours is read as one event, sized exactly to remove the excess; every other shape installs nothing.
eq_title: Interval $i$ runs from expiry $i-1$ to expiry $i$ and spans $d_i$ calendar days
eq_labels: 1 · Forward variance per calendar year: fixed by prices
2 · Reference: the hotter neighbour, read on the event clock
3 · Event size: the extra days that bring $f_i$ down to $r_i$
4 · Materiality: both floors, or no event
eq_note: $w_i$: ATM total variance of expiry $i$ from its fitted slice, the same on both clocks. $t_i$, $\tau_i$: calendar and event-clock times; $f^{\tau}_j$ includes the events already found, so the rule repeats until no peak is left.
paras: Peaks only
an event can only lower its own interval's event-clock rate. A ramp, a smooth backwardation or a dip cannot come from an event: nothing is installed.
Ends and placement

the last interval is never a candidate; the first compares with its right neighbour, extended by the back ladder's slope when that ladder falls. An event goes at its interval's midpoint; edit the date if you know it.

head: Interval (days)
ATM vol at its end, calendar
Forward vol $\sqrt{f_i}$
Found $N_i$

example: Monthly ladder, 20% on the event clock, earnings worth 4 extra days between days 30 and 60. That interval is hotter than both neighbours: $N = 30\,(0.04533/0.04 - 1) = 4.0$ days. The Ladder spread readout goes from 53 variance bp on the calendar clock to 0 on the event clock.
notes: The previous slide took the event calendar as given. This one reads it off the market. The input is the at-the-money total variance of each calibrated expiry, taken from each slice's LQD backbone.
The first line is the forward variance of each interval between two expiries, per calendar year. Prices fix it, so no calendar can change it. The information is in how uneven this ladder is.

The key fact is a sign. An event inside an interval adds days to that interval on the event clock. That lowers the interval's event-clock forward variance and leaves every other interval alone. So the only shape an event can create is a peak: an interval running hotter than both neighbours. A rising ramp, a smooth decline, a dip: no event produces those, so the rule installs nothing for them. It is a detector, not a smoother.

The second and third lines. The reference is the hotter of the two neighbours, read on the event clock, so it includes any event already found there. Now ask for the extra days that make this interval run exactly at its reference. The interval's variance increment, divided by its days plus the extra days, must equal the reference. That solves to the third line. The size is exact, with no penalty shrinking it. Clipping one peak can lower a neighbour's reference, so the rule repeats until no peak is left. It converges to the smallest events that leave no peak, in at most one pass per interval. That takes microseconds.

The fourth line is materiality. An event must add at least half a day, and at least 3 percent of the interval's days. On a monthly interval the second floor binds, at 0.9 of a day. Fit noise between adjacent expiries sits below both floors; an earnings day sits far above.

The table. A monthly ladder at 20 percent on the event clock, with earnings worth four extra days inside the second month. On the calendar clock the ATM vols read 20.00, 20.66, 20.44 and 20.33 percent: the familiar hump. The forward vols read 20, then 21.29, then 20 and 20. The second interval is hotter than both neighbours. Its size is 30 times 0.04533 over 0.04 minus one: 4.0 days, placed at day 45, the midpoint. After installing it the event-clock ladder is flat, and the Ladder spread readout goes from 53 variance basis points to zero.

The two ends. The last interval has no right neighbour, so it is never a candidate. It is the reference for the tail, whatever horizon you choose. The first interval has no left neighbour, so its reference is the second interval, extended one step by the back ladder's own slope when that ladder is falling. A volatility spike that decays smoothly is therefore not read as an event.

Placement is a convention. Prices only see the total variance at each listed expiry. They cannot tell Tuesday from Thursday inside one interval, nor two events from one event of their combined size. The midpoint is a default; the date is yours to edit.

On real data, the 18 July AAPL export with four expiries: one event of 3.8 days in the September to December interval, and nothing elsewhere. That interval contains the late-October earnings. The ladder spread fell from 127 to 106 variance basis points. On SPY it installs nothing.
Transition: the clock handles time. Next: what happens to a stored fit when spot moves between calibrations.

If asked why not fit a smooth clock: the earlier version minimised a flatness objective. It put events on ramps, read mild backwardation as events and stopped early. It was replaced on 4 September by this detector, which installs events only where an event is the one explanation of the shape.

If asked about its limits: two adjacent events of equal size form a plateau, which has no peak and is invisible. The first interval cannot separate a scheduled event from a spike front that decays faster than the back ladder. And the detector reads the ATM ladder only. Review the installed calendar before relying on it.
demo: Parametric ▸ Term ▸ Auto-calibrate events: choose the horizon, then Calibrate; read the result line and the Ladder spread readout, calendar clock then event clock. Uncalibrated expiries are skipped, so light the ladder first.

title: Spot transport between calibrations
lede: Between calibrations the stored fit is read through a transport, not refitted; the spot–vol rule $R$ of slide 5 sets how far the smile slides.
eq_title: Forward move $h = \log(F_1/F_0)$; $R$ is the spot–vol rule
eq_labels: 1 · The new curve reads the stored one $Rh$ further along; a fixed strike's label moves by $-h$
2 · ATM response, to first order
3 · Sticky local vol: Hagan's map, $w_1(k) = w_0(\ell(k,h))$
eq_note: $F_0$, $F_1$: stored and current forward; $w_0$, $\sigma_0$: stored variance and vol; $s_0 = \partial_k\sigma_0(0)$: ATM skew; $\tau$ is unchanged.
paras: The dial $R$
0 sticky moneyness, the smile rides the forward; 1 sticky strike, the default: every strike keeps its vol; 2 sticky local vol: at the money the curve slides twice as far, $\ell(0,h) \simeq 2h$.
Hagan's map

in a local-vol model the implied vol at $K$ is, to leading order, the local vol at the midpoint $(F+K)/2$. Freeze the local-vol surface in strike: the new smile at $K$ reads the stored one at the strike with the same midpoint against $F_0$, which is $\ell$.
What is recomputed
nothing: every view reads the stored fit through the map, no PDE; only the Scenario overlay's LV-grid regime reprices through Dupire, on a grid taken from the parametric smiles.
alt: Illustrative smile read after a 2% forward fall under R equal to zero, one and two
caption: Three readings of one stored smile: $\sigma_0(k) = 0.20 - 0.30k + 0.35k^2$ after a 2% forward fall, $h = -0.02$. Each curve is the stored one shifted right by $0.02R$; with a negative skew the ATM vol rises with $R$.
example: The new ATM reads the stored curve at $Rh$. $R = 1$: $\sigma_0(-0.02) = 20.61\%$, +61 bp (first order +60). $R = 2$: $\sigma_0(-0.04) = 21.26\%$, +126 bp; Hagan's map, $\ell(0,h) = -0.0404$, gives +127 bp.
notes: A calibration is a snapshot at one spot. Between calibrations spot moves, every forward moves with it, and the app has to show a smile at the new forward without refitting. How the smile moves with spot is not in today's quotes. Through every arbitrage-free surface pass many admissible tomorrows. So it is a choice: the spot–vol rule, R on this slide. It is the same rule as in quote synchronisation, earlier in the deck.

The move is h, the log of the new forward over the stored fit's forward. It is positive when the forward rises. It is always computed from forwards. Under a cash dividend schedule the forward moves additively: the new forward is the stored forward plus the spot change, grown at the rate. So the move differs from one expiry to the next.

The first line: the new curve at a given log-moneyness reads the stored curve further along, by the rule times the move. The variance time does not change, so this is also a horizontal slide of the vol curve. The second half of the line is the check on the signs. A fixed strike does not move, but its log-moneyness does, by minus the move. Substitute, and its variance becomes the stored curve read at the old log-moneyness plus the rule minus one, times the move. With the rule at one, the argument is the old log-moneyness: every fixed strike keeps its vol. That is sticky strike, exactly, and it is the default. With the rule at zero the curve does not move in log-moneyness: the smile rides the forward. That is sticky moneyness.

The second line: at the money, the new vol is the stored curve read at the rule times the move. To first order it moves by the rule, times the skew, times the move. That is what makes the rule the skew-stickiness ratio: the ATM vol change per unit move of the log-forward, divided by the skew. Equity skew is negative. So when the forward falls, the ATM vol rises for any positive value of the rule.

The third line is sticky local vol, and here is what Hagan's map is. In a local-volatility model, Hagan's expansion says the implied vol at a strike is, to leading order, the local vol at the midpoint between the forward and the strike. Now freeze the local-vol surface in absolute strike and move the forward. The new implied vol at a strike is the local vol at the midpoint between the new forward and that strike. That is the old implied vol at the strike whose midpoint with the old forward is the same point. Write that strike in log-moneyness and you get the map, ell on the slide. The stored smile is read at the mapped log-moneyness: a nonlinear relabelling instead of the straight slide of the first line. At the money the map gives about twice the move. The curve slides twice as far, which is where a rule near two comes from: short-dated implied skew is about half the local skew. Away from the money the displacement is larger on the put side; the factor on the slide, one plus the exponential of minus k, says by how much.

What is recomputed on a spot move: nothing. The fitted parameters stay exactly as calibrated. Every view reads the stored fit through the transport: the smile, the term structure, the density, the variance swap, the local-vol extraction. For the two local-vol regimes that transport is Hagan's map, a closed form, not a PDE. The calibrated affine surface, when there is one, is transported the same way: its reconstructed smiles go through the map, and its vertex grid is relabelled. With the rule at two the grid stays fixed in absolute strike. Calibrate refits and resets the move to zero.

The one place where the PDE is re-run is the Scenario overlay of the Parametric lens, in the LV-grid regime. It extracts a local-vol grid from the fitted parametric smiles, with Dupire's formula on the parametric surface. It holds that grid fixed in absolute strike, reprices the expiry through the forward PDE, and reports the realised rule as an output. In the recorded test that was 2.09 at seven weeks and 2.00 at eighteen months. It needs no local-vol calibration. If the node has no parametric fit at all, there is nothing to transport and the overlay is empty.

The worked example. The plotted smile, with the forward down two percent. Sticky strike: the new ATM reads the old curve at minus 0.02, 20.61 percent. That is 60 basis points from the skew and 1.4 from the curvature. Sticky local vol, linear: read at minus 0.04, 21.26 percent. Hagan's map reads at minus 0.0404: plus 127 bp. And the old ATM strike, now at a log-moneyness of plus 0.02, keeps 20 percent only under sticky strike. It reads 19.41 with the rule at zero and 20.61 with the rule at two.
Transition: the same transport brings yesterday's saved fit to today's forward. That is where the prior starts: next slide.

If asked why the choice matters: hedge ratios. A fixed strike's vol moves by the rule minus one, times the skew, per unit move of the log-forward, so the delta changes by vega times that. On a recorded long-dated SPY smile with a skew of minus 0.354, the gap between a rule of zero and a rule of two is 19.7 delta points. That is on an out-of-the-money put: same book, same surface.

If asked what happens if local volatility was never calibrated: nothing changes. The two local-vol regimes only need the stored parametric smile, read through Hagan's map. The Scenario's LV-grid regime builds its grid from the parametric smiles. The affine local-vol calibration is never required for a transport.

If asked about the other regimes in the Scenario overlay: for moneyness, strike and the linear local-vol rule it uses a one-line formula in vol space. The curve is re-indexed by the move, then shifted in level by the rule minus one, times the skew, times the move. Its ATM response matches to first order; in the wings it differs at second order. For large moves all of these are first-order rules. The recorded test measured up to 111 vol basis points between Hagan's map and the linear rule at two, in the wings of a 5 percent move.
demo: Spot move card ▸ Scenario: the dial moves the spot and every lens reads the transported fit; Options ▸ Spot-vol dynamics switches the regime.

title: Activating a prior where quote support is weak
lede: Yesterday's smile may pull on today's fit only where today's quotes leave a feature undetermined. Each persisted feature has a gate: fully open with no nearby quote, exactly closed from about one quote on.
eq_title: Per expiry: operators ATM, RR25, BF25 with legs $k_a$ on the transported prior
eq_labels: 1 · Support of a leg: effective number of quotes near it
2 · Information of an operator, $I_{\mathrm{ATM}} = n_0$: every leg must be supported
3 · Gate: 1 with no support, exactly 0 from the required level
4 · One row per open gate; rows share a budget
paras: Order
transport the saved prior to today's forward (previous slide), place the legs on it once, measure support from today's quotes, then gate.
A closed gate is exact
$g_j = 0$ gives $\Lambda_j = 0$: the row adds no cost and no gradient, so the prior cannot pull on a feature the quotes pin down. Support counts quotes; it does not check that they agree.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: Log-moneyness of quote $i$; its fit weight rescaled to mean one
Support at the ATM leg and at the $25\Delta$ call and put legs
Information of operator $j$; required level 1, one effective quote
Gate, the gap column in the app; sharpness, 1
The operator, in vol, on the model's smile and on the transported prior
Weight of prior row $j$ (column $\lambda$ in the app); budget $B = 50\% \times \sum_i \lambda_i$
Gate of the var-swap level: its own row, weight $B\,g_{\mathrm{VS}}$, support probed at 0 and $\pm 1.4\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ATM}}\sqrt{\tau}$

example: One-year node, flat 20% prior, five equal-weight quotes at $k = 0, \pm 0.02, \pm 0.04$: $B = 2.5$. Supports $n_0 = 4.49$, $n_c = 0.30$ ($k = 0.155$), $n_p = 1.02$ ($k = -0.115$). ATM closed. RR: $I = 0.23$, $g = 0.77$, $\Lambda = 1.91$. BF: $I = 0.76$, $g = 0.24$, $\Lambda = 0.59$. Var swap: $g = 1$, weight 2.5.
notes: Overnight the at-the-money level moves on news and is re-quoted at once. The wings may get no fresh quote at all. Fit today's quotes alone and the unquoted wings flap. Anchor everything to yesterday and the prior damps the genuine move at the money. The rule of this slide: yesterday may speak only where today is silent.

The set-up. The saved prior is first carried to today's forward with the transport of the previous slide. So a pure spot move is not mistaken for a change of shape. The persisted features are operators, the desk's own coordinates: the ATM vol, the 25-delta risk reversal and butterfly, and the variance-swap level. Their leg strikes are located once, on the transported prior, and frozen.

The first line is support. For each leg, count today's quotes near it with a Gaussian kernel of width 0.06 in log-moneyness, with the fit weights rescaled to mean one. A quote exactly on the leg counts one. A quote two bandwidths away counts about 0.14.

The second line is the information of an operator. Suppose each leg's vol were estimated independently, with a variance proportional to one over its support. Then the operator's variance would be the sum of its coefficients squared over the supports, and the information is the inverse. Two consequences. One unsupported leg kills the operator: a risk reversal with no put quotes is undetermined, however many calls there are. And the butterfly's wing legs enter with a quarter, so the same legs identify the butterfly more easily than the risk reversal.

The third line is the gate. It is one when there is no support. It falls linearly, with the sharpness at one, and it is exactly zero once the information reaches the requirement: one effective quote. Exactly zero, not small.

The fourth line is the rows. Each open gate adds one residual row. It is the operator on the model's smile, minus the same operator on the transported prior, in vol, times the square root of its weight. The weights share a budget, B on the slide: 50 percent of the summed quote weights by default, split in proportion to the gates. The variance-swap operator has its own row, with weight equal to the budget times its gate. Its support is probed at the money and 1.4 ATM standard deviations out on each side.

The worked example. A one-year node, a flat 20 percent prior, five quotes of weight one within four hundredths of the money, so the budget is 2.5. The prior rows together weigh like two and a half quotes. The ATM leg has 4.49 effective quotes: closed. The 25-delta call leg at 0.155 has 0.30; the put leg at minus 0.115 has 1.02. The risk reversal's information is 0.23, its gate 0.77, its weight 1.91. The butterfly's information is 0.76, its gate 0.24, its weight 0.59. The variance swap sees almost nothing at 0.28 from the money: gate one, weight 2.5.

The flip side. The same five quotes on a three-month node close every vol gate. The 25-delta legs sit at plus 0.07 and minus 0.06, about one bandwidth from the quotes, and the kernel credits them. Only the variance-swap row stays open, with a gate of 0.77. The kernel overstates identification just beyond the last quote. That is why the default mode, hybrid, adds strike anchors for the deep tail: next slide.

What a closed gate guarantees: a zero row, so no cost and no gradient. The prior cannot pull on that feature directly. It can still move it indirectly, through other open rows and the model's own coupling. And support counts quotes; it does not check whether they agree. Disagreement is the Kalman filter's business, two slides on.
Transition: which features to persist matters as much as where. Shape against level, next slide.

If asked where the prior comes from: one prior per node, active on save. Saving a node's fit makes it the prior at once, with no fetch step. Only lit, calibrated nodes can become priors; graph output never does. There is no age decay in this gate.

If asked whether the gate could use the real precision of the fit: the opt-in two-pass mode does that. It fits once without the prior, measures how well each operator is actually pinned, then refits. That is exact, at about twice the cost.
demo: Options ▸ Prior ▸ Config: the Prior diagnostics table lists, per expiry, the open operators with gap · $\lambda$ · age · src · $h$. An operator the quotes pin down drops out of the table.

title: Persisting shape versus absolute strike values
lede: What the prior persists decides which moves it resists: risk reversals and butterflies ignore a parallel shift of the smile; a fixed-strike anchor does not.
eq_title: Legs at the $25\Delta$ call and put strikes $k_c$, $k_p$, frozen on the transported prior
eq_labels: 1 · Shape operators: coefficients that sum to zero
2 · So a parallel move by $v$ vol points leaves both unchanged
3 · Strike anchor: a price residual over vega, read in vol
eq_note: $k_\Delta = \tfrac12\sigma^2\tau - \sigma\sqrt{\tau}\,N^{-1}(\Delta)$: strike of forward call delta $\Delta$ (0.25 call, 0.75 put). $c$: call price in forward units. $\Lambda_j$: row weight (previous slide).
paras: Hybrid, the default

ATM, RR25, BF25 and the var-swap level carry shape where their gates open; anchors at the $2\Delta$, $5\Delta$ and $10\Delta$ strikes hold the deep tail no operator reaches. The anchor rows share a budget of 20% of the node's summed quote weights $\sum_i \lambda_i$, split by each anchor's missing quote mass: zero where quotes already cover it.
Across a jump
a shape row follows today's level; a strike anchor pulls the unquoted wing back toward yesterday's absolute vol.
alt: Illustrative smiles: an earlier smile, the same shape lifted by four points, and a fit that keeps the earlier wings outside the quoted band
caption: Illustrative: the whole smile lifted by 4 points keeps its RR and BF at fixed legs. A fit anchored to the earlier absolute wings keeps the old level outside the quoted band (shaded).
example: Yesterday ATM 20%, $25\Delta$ call 19%, put 23%: $\mathrm{RR} = -4$, $\mathrm{BF} = +1$ vol point. Overnight every vol rises 4 points: 24%, 23%, 27%. RR and BF are unchanged, so their rows cost nothing. A strike anchor there, as in strike-gap mode, still targets 23%: a 4-point residual pulling the wing down.
reference: Note 13 · operator invariance and strike anchors
notes: The gate decides where the prior may pull. This slide is about what it pulls on, and that decides which market moves the prior resists.

The first line: the risk reversal and the butterfly, with legs at the 25-delta strikes, located once on the transported prior and frozen. Their coefficients are plus one and minus one for the risk reversal; one half, one half and minus one for the butterfly. Both sets sum to zero.

The second line is the consequence. Add the same amount to every vol and both operators are unchanged. A shape row therefore cannot resist a parallel move. When the at-the-money quotes lift the level overnight, the rows carry yesterday's shape onto today's level. The unquoted wing is rebuilt as today's ATM plus yesterday's shape.

The third line is the other kind of row, the strike anchor. It is a call-price difference at a fixed strike, divided by the prior's vega plus a floor, so it reads as a vol error. It persists an absolute value at that strike. If the level jumps and that strike is unquoted, the anchor pulls the wing back toward yesterday's absolute vol. The inverse vega is capped at 25 times its smallest value, so a far-tail anchor cannot dominate.

The worked example. Yesterday: ATM 20, the 25-delta call 19, the put 23. Risk reversal minus 4, butterfly plus 1. Overnight every vol rises by 4 points. The risk reversal and the butterfly are unchanged, so their rows cost nothing. An anchor at the put strike still targets 23 against a market at 27: a 4-point residual pulling the wing down. The figure shows the same thing on a whole curve.

On a recorded, controlled 4-point jump with quotes only near the money, the operator rows land 0.3 vol point from the lifted wing. That is at a log-moneyness of minus 0.20. Strike anchors miss it by 3.7, still 3.3 from yesterday's curve. And the at-the-money fit under the operator prior matches the data-only fit to 0.00: no damping where the quotes are.

Why the default combines both. Pure operator modes are often inert on liquid mornings: the kernel closes their gates, as on the previous slide. And no operator reaches the deep tail. Hybrid adds strike anchors at the 2, 5 and 10-delta strikes of the transported prior. Their budget: together, the anchor rows get a total least-squares weight equal to 20 percent of the node's summed quote weights. That is the setting priorTailAnchorStrengthPct, and it makes the prior compete with the data at a controlled strength. The total is split among the anchors in proportion to the missing quote mass in each anchor's cell. That mass is the desired quote density minus the observed one, floored at zero, times the cell width. An anchor sitting where the quotes already reach gets nothing. As the data fill in, the rows vanish. On the August 2024 spike backtest, over 1,116 node-days, hybrid improved the held-out wing by a median 32 vol basis points over no prior. It won 66 percent of the days. The pure operator modes were at zero at the median. The price: across a jump, the deep tail is still pulled toward yesterday's absolute level.
Transition: the prior fills gaps. Next: dense but noisy quotes, where the gate is closed and yet today's fit should not be taken at face value. That is the Kalman filter.

If asked how to see the effect on one node: the chart header's Fit switch draws a shadow fit in place of production. Free is the fit with no prior and no filter, on the same quotes and model. With a saved prior active, production is the plus-Prior fit. Parametric Compare adds the Pull column: the ATM distance to the free fit, in vol basis points.

If asked about the variance-swap row: it matches the prior's variance-swap level by default. An option makes it match the variance swap minus the ATM vol instead, so a level move carries the tail along.
demo: On a thin node with a saved prior: the chart header's Fit switch, Production (the + Prior fit) against Free; Parametric ▸ Compare shows the Pull column in ATM vol bp.

title: Temporal filtering of ATM handles
lede: Each calibration is a noisy reading of three numbers: ATM level, skew and curvature. The filter carries yesterday's estimate to today and averages it with today's reading, each weighted by the inverse of its variance.
eq_title: Per node, one scalar filter for each handle $x \in \{\sigma_0, s_0, \kappa_0\}$
eq_labels: 1 · Predict: move the last estimate to today's forward; the wait adds variance
2 · Measure: today's fit reads the handle as $z$, with a variance $R$ built on the next slide
3 · Update: the inverse-variance average of prediction and reading
4 · The transport of the three handles, first order in the forward move $h$
paras: Never a setting
the gain follows from the two variances. A precise reading, small $R$, moves the estimate almost fully; a wide one barely.
Per handle
the three updates are separate: on coarse chains, correlations between level and curvature let a junk curvature reading drag the level by 3 to 28 vol points.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: ATM vol, skew $\partial_k\sigma(0)$ and curvature $\partial_k^2\sigma(0)$ of the LQD fit (slide 17)
Predicted value and variance of a handle, before today's reading
Its filtered value and variance after the reading
Today's fitted handle and its variance, from the fit itself (next slide)
Variance added by the wait: $(30\ \text{bp})^2$ per day for the level, $0.02^2$ and $0.05^2$ per day for skew and curvature, plus a term in the spot move
The gain: the share of the total variance the prediction carries; 0 keeps the prediction, 1 takes the reading
Log forward move since the last reading; the spot–vol rule of slide 31, written SSR here because $R$ is a variance

example: Level: prediction $20.0\% \pm 0.30\%$, today's fit $20.4\% \pm 0.15\%$: $K = 0.30^2/(0.30^2 + 0.15^2) = 0.80$, posterior $20.32\% \pm 0.13\%$. Curvature: prediction $0.10 \pm 0.05$, fit $0.55 \pm 0.30$ (a stale strike puts a kink in it): $K = 0.027$, posterior $0.112$. The kink is barely admitted.
notes: The prior of the last two slides fills gaps. This slide is about the opposite case: dense quotes, so every gate is closed, but noisy ones. Today's fit should not be taken at face value. The tool is a Kalman filter on three numbers per node, the ATM handles: level, skew and curvature.

The principle in one sentence: two estimates of the same number, each with a variance, are best combined by weighting each with the inverse of its variance. The filter does that once per day, per node and per handle.

The first line is the prediction. Take the last filtered value and move it to today's forward with the transport of the fourth line. That is the same spot rule as on the transport slide, to first order. Its variance grows by Q on the slide, the variance the wait adds. By default that is 30 vol basis points per root day for the level, plus a term for the size of the spot move.

The second line is the measurement. Today's data-only fit gives each handle a value, the reading, z on the slide. It also gives the reading's variance, R on the slide, and that is the part that is computed, not set. The next slide builds the reading's variance from the fit itself.

The third line is the update. The posterior is the inverse-variance average: the reading's variance times the prediction, plus the prediction's variance times the reading, over their sum. Written as a step, it moves the prediction toward the reading by the gain, K on the slide. The gain is the prediction's share of the total variance. And the precisions add: the posterior precision is the prediction's precision plus the reading's precision. A precise reading, with a small variance, gives a gain near one and the reading wins. A noisy one gives a small gain and the estimate barely moves.

The fourth line is the transport of the three handles. The level moves by the spot rule, times the skew, times the forward move. The skew moves by the curvature times the forward move. The curvature stays. The spot rule is written SSR on these two slides, because here R is the reading's variance.

The updates run per handle, separately, and that is deliberate. With a full three-by-three covariance, the correlation between level and curvature let a junk curvature reading on a coarse chain drag the level. In the backtest that was by 3 to 28 vol points, worse than no filter at all. Scalar gains cannot do that.

The worked example. The level's prediction is 20.0 plus or minus 0.30, and the fit reads 20.4 plus or minus 0.15. The gain is 0.09 over 0.1125, which is 0.80, so the posterior is 20.32 plus or minus 0.13. For the curvature, a stale strike has put a kink in today's fit: it reads 0.55 against a prediction of 0.10. But its variance is so much wider that the gain is 0.027. The posterior is 0.112: the kink is barely admitted.
Transition: everything rests on the reading's variance, R on the slide. The next slide shows how it is built from the fit itself.

If asked how this differs from the prior: the prior has a gate and turns off where the quotes speak. The filter is always on, at a weight that follows from the variances. And the prior acts on the fit, while the filter, in its default overlay mode, acts on the handles read off the fit.

title: Where the reading's variance comes from
lede: The variance of today's handles is computed from the fit itself: from how firmly the quotes, at their stated noise, pin the parameters, and from how badly the fit missed them.
eq_title: Today's fit: parameters $\theta$, $m$ quotes, handles $x(\theta) = (\sigma_0, s_0, \kappa_0)$
eq_labels: 1 · Stated noise of a quote, in vol: half its spread, floored at 1 bp, wider under 30 days
2 · How firmly the quotes pin the parameters: the Jacobian, each quote row divided by its noise
3 · From parameters to handles: the handle Jacobian $G$ carries the uncertainty through
4 · Inflate when the fit misses the quotes by more than their stated noise
eq: \mathcal{I}_\theta=J^\top J,\qquad J_{ij}=\frac{1}{\delta_i}\,\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial\theta_j}\ \ \text{(quote rows)},\ \ \text{plus the penalty rows}
eq_note: $r_i$: residual of quote $i$ in vol (slide 10), $\lambda_i$ its weight (slide 12), both at the solution. $J$: one row per quote and per penalty, one column per parameter. $\mathcal{I}_\theta^{-1}$: regularised — eigenvalues under $10^{-10}$ of the largest are raised, so an unpinned direction reads as a large, finite variance. $n_d$: calendar days to expiry.
paras: Reading the Jacobian

$J^\top J$ says how much a unit move of each parameter would change the residuals, in units of the quotes' noise: large means pinned. $G$ says how much each handle moves per parameter. $G\,\mathcal{I}^{-1}G^\top$ is then the variance of the handles that the quote noise implies.
Contradiction is noise
a cluster the fit cannot match within its stated noise raises $\chi^2$, so $\rho$ and $R$ grow and the gain falls, with no threshold.
Overlay or active

Overlay, the default, computes and draws the filtered handles; the fit is untouched. Active adds the prediction to the fit as three rows $(x_j(\theta) - m_j^-)^2/P_j^-$, and the fit's own handles become the posterior.
example: Twenty quotes, each with 10 bp of stated noise, all reading the level: $\mathcal{I} \approx 20/\delta^2$, so the level's sd is $\delta/\sqrt{20} = 2.2$ bp. If the fit misses them by twice their noise, $\chi^2 \approx 80$ and $\rho \approx 80/17 = 4.7$: the sd becomes $2.2\sqrt{4.7} = 4.9$ bp and the gain falls.
notes: Everything on the previous slide rests on the reading's variance, R on the slide. Quote weights cannot give it. They say which quotes matter more, not how noisy each one is. So the reading's variance is built from three things: the market's stated noise per quote, the fit's own sensitivities, and how badly the fit missed.

The first line is the stated noise. Each quote gets half its bid–ask spread in vol, floored at one basis point. Below 30 days it is multiplied by the square root of 30 over the days to expiry: 1.4 at 15 days, 2 at 7 days. That is because short-dated quotes were measured to be two to three times noisier than their spread says.

The second line is the Jacobian. It is the matrix the solver already has at the solution. There is one row per quote, holding the derivative of that quote's residual with respect to every parameter, plus the model's penalty rows. Divide each quote row by its noise. The Jacobian transposed times itself is then the information matrix. Entry by entry, it says how much a unit move of the parameters changes the residuals, measured in units of the quotes' noise. A direction the quotes pin has a large entry. A direction they do not see has a small one. In band mode a quote sitting inside its spread has a zero row: it contributes no information, which is right.

The third line goes from parameters to handles. The handle Jacobian, G on the slide, has three rows, one per handle, and one column per parameter. It says how much the ATM level, skew and curvature move when each parameter moves. It is computed by central differences of the exact handle map, each evaluation a slice build, so microseconds. The delta method then gives the handles' variance: the handle Jacobian, times the inverse information, times the handle Jacobian transposed. The inverse is regularised. Eigenvalues below ten to the minus ten of the largest are raised, so an unpinned direction reads as a large but finite variance, never as zero uncertainty.

The fourth line is the inflation. Chi-square is the fit's weighted misfit in units of the stated noise, summed over the quotes. If the fit sits inside the stated noise, chi-square over the degrees of freedom is about one and nothing changes. If a dense cluster cannot be fitted within its stated noise, the quotes contradict each other. Then chi-square grows, the inflation factor, rho on the slide, grows, the reading's variance grows, and the gain falls. No threshold, no rule: disagreement among the quotes reads as noise. The inflation factor is capped at 25, so one broken chain cannot poison the state.

The worked example gives the shape of the numbers. Twenty quotes, 10 basis points of noise each, all reading the level. The information is 20 over the noise squared, so the level's standard deviation is the noise over the square root of 20: 2.2 bp. If the fit misses every quote by twice its noise, chi-square is about 80 over 17 degrees of freedom. The inflation factor is then 4.7, and the standard deviation becomes 4.9 bp. In the recorded test, a contradictory cluster took the curvature gain from 0.73 to 0.20 and left the level's gain at 0.74.

Overlay and active. In Overlay, the default, the filter computes the posterior handles and draws them. The fit itself is untouched, and the filtered smile is the fit retargeted to the posterior handles. In Active, the prediction enters the fit as three extra rows: each handle's distance to its prediction, over the prediction's variance. One calibration then produces the posterior directly, and today's quotes count once. Prior rows on the same handles are dropped in that case.
Transition: to compare the free, prior and filtered fits through time on the same observations, the app replays stored frames. The Series lens, next.

If asked about the factors route: when no solver Jacobian is available, the covariance falls back to the graph layer's precision vocabulary, per handle. That is rms, quote density, spread and freshness. It is also the A/B column in the filter table.

If asked about intraday use: at daily cadence, on expiries beyond 30 days, the active fit beat both the raw fit and the overlay in the backtest. On intraday series with short expiries it did not. An active lane spent minutes per frame and diverged, so the Series dialog warns and caps a frame at 300 seconds. Overlay has no such problem.

title: Series replay and independent calibration lanes
lede: A series stores one ticker's chains at a sequence of instants. Several lanes calibrate the same frames in time order, each with its own settings and its own memory, so their differences come from the settings alone.
eq_title: Lane $\ell$ over frames $i = 1 \ldots n$, for the expiry on screen
eq_labels: 1 · Memory: a lane's prior is its own previous fit, transported
2 · Fit error: mean over frames of the fit's RMS, in vol bp
3 · Roughness: mean frame-to-frame move of the ATM vol
4 · Pull: ATM distance to the free lane at the same frame
eq_note: $\mathcal T_h$: the spot transport of slide 31. $F_i$: the expiry's forward at frame $i$. $\sigma_0^{\ell}(i)$: ATM vol of lane $\ell$ at frame $i$. A free lane has no memory; a filter lane also carries its own Kalman state, and $\zeta = (z - m^-)/\sqrt{P^- + R}$ has a spread near 1 when its variances are right.
paras: Three questions

fit to the quotes of each frame (rms), stability through time (roughness), and response to a real move. A prior or a filter buys stability at some rms; a smoother path alone does not prove a better estimate.
Presets
LQD free, + prior (hybrid), + prior + filter (active), SVI-JW free, MCS free, LV free, LV + prior, and Current Options. A memory lane's first frame is a seed fit.

example: 25 frames, 15 minutes apart; one-day expiry. Free: rms 4.66 bp, ATM roughness 18.4 bp per frame. + Prior (hybrid): rms 5.20 bp, roughness 17.5 bp, mean $|\mathrm{pull}|$ 3.6 bp. The overlay filter leaves the fit unchanged and adds its record: ATM $\zeta$ standard deviation 0.82.
notes: Everything in this chapter has a time dimension. The prior uses yesterday; the filter carries a state. Judging them needs the same observations run under different settings, in time order. That is what a series does.

Frames first. A series has one ticker, a clock, meaning a start, a step and a count, and a ladder of expiries. Each frame is the chain at one instant. It is harvested from Massive's historical NBBO, the same as-of fetch as the Smile lens, at about 12 seconds per frame under the 1,500-contract cap. Or it is taken live at each tick, or imported from stored captures. A frame is an observation: nothing is interpolated between frames.

Lanes. Each lane is a patch over the series' base settings, frozen at creation, so the replay is reproducible after the live Options change. The presets: LQD free; plus prior, which is hybrid; plus prior plus filter, which is the active filter. Then SVI-JW free and MCS free, local vol free and with prior, and Current Options, the live settings as they are. Each lane runs on its own detached state. The live desk is never touched.

The first line is memory. A prior lane's prior at one frame is its own fit at the previous frame, carried to the new forward by the spot transport from earlier in this chapter. Its filter state is also its own, with the time step read off the snapshot timestamps. A free lane has no memory: its frames are independent. The first frame of a memory lane is a seed fit. The carry is checkpointed at every frame, so pause and resume reproduce the same fits.
Order: every lane fits a frame before any lane moves to the next one. The harvest runs in its own thread, so a frame's fits start as soon as its chain lands.

The second to fourth lines are the readouts. Mean rms: the fit's error to that frame's quotes, averaged over the frames. Roughness: the average absolute frame-to-frame move of the ATM vol, which is what a prior or a filter damps. Pull: the lane's ATM vol minus the free lane's at the same frame, which is what the prior bought. Read them together. A prior that lowers roughness for a small rms cost is doing its job. One that lowers roughness by lagging a real move is not. Look at the frames around the move.

The recorded example, from a SPY replay day on 10 September: 25 frames, 15 minutes apart, on the one-day expiry. Free: rms 4.66 basis points, roughness 18.4 bp per frame. Plus prior: rms 5.20, roughness 17.5, mean absolute pull 3.6 bp. So the prior damps the path by about 0.9 bp per frame, for about half a bp of rms. The overlay filter leaves the fit unchanged and adds its record, with an ATM zeta standard deviation of 0.82.

The filter lane in that readout had to be the overlay filter. The plus-prior-plus-filter preset uses the active filter, which the previous slide showed failing at intraday cadence on short expiries. Series creation warns, and a 300-second frame budget stops a lane from diverging for ever. For filter evidence on an intraday series, set Options to hybrid with the filter on Overlay, and add the Current Options lane.

Adopting a result is explicit. Adopt as prior saves one lane's fit at one frame as the live prior, through the normal save route. Nothing else in a series writes a prior. A series can be exported to a file and imported elsewhere.
Transition: so far each node has been handled alone, through time. The last chapter couples nodes across expiries and underlyings: the graph.

If asked whether a lane reproduces the desk: yes. A free lane's frame fit is byte-identical to a desk Calibrate on the same chain under the same settings, and a test locks that. The certification case for series replay determinism re-runs a stored series and reproduces every fit.

If asked about cost: measured on the stored 0DTE store, a free LQD lane took 391 milliseconds per frame, 28 seconds for 60 frames. A hybrid-prior lane took 1,266 milliseconds per frame at the median. Local-vol lanes dominate, at 1 to 25 seconds per frame.
